Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

This paper considers the propagation of shallow-water solitary and nonlinear periodic waves over a gradual slope with bottom friction in the framework of a variable-coefficient Korteweg-de Vries equation. We use the Whitham averaging method, using a recent development of this theory for perturbed integrable equations. This general approach enables us not only to improve known results on the adiabatic evolution of isolated solitary waves and periodic wave trains in the presence of variable topography and bottom friction, modeled by the Chezy law, but also importantly, to study the effects of these factors on the propagation of undular bores, which are essentially unsteady in the system under consideration. In particular, it is shown that the combined action of variable topography and bottom friction generally imposes certain global restrictions on the undular bore propagation so that the evolution of the leading solitary wave can be substantially different from that of an isolated solitary wave with the same initial amplitude. This non-local effect is due to nonlinear wave interactions within the undular bore and can lead to an additional solitary wave amplitude growth, which cannot be predicted in the framework of the traditional adiabatic approach to the propagation of solitary waves in slowly varying media.

outputs.L1: This paper examines the propagation of shallow-water solitary and nonlinear periodic waves over a gradual slope with bottom friction, within the framework of a variable-coefficient Korteweg–de Vries equation. We employ the Whitham averaging method, drawing on recent developments in this theory for perturbed integrable equations. This general approach enables us not only to refine existing results on the adiabatic evolution of isolated solitary waves and periodic wave trains in the presence of variable topography and bottom friction, modeled by the Chézy law, but also, importantly, to investigate the effects of these factors on the propagation of undular bores, which are intrinsically unsteady in the system under consideration. In particular, we show that the combined action of variable topography and bottom friction generally imposes certain global restrictions on undular bore propagation, such that the evolution of the leading solitary wave can differ substantially from that of an isolated solitary wave with the same initial amplitude. This nonlocal effect arises from nonlinear wave interactions within the undular bore and can lead to additional growth of the solitary-wave amplitude, a phenomenon that cannot be predicted within the traditional adiabatic framework for solitary-wave propagation in slowly varying media.
outputs.L2: This study examines how shallow-water solitary waves and nonlinear periodic waves travel across a gently varying slope when bottom friction is present, using a variable-coefficient Korteweg–de Vries equation as the model. The analysis applies the Whitham averaging technique, specifically drawing on recent extensions of that theory for perturbed integrable systems. This broader framework allows the authors to refine existing results concerning the adiabatic evolution of individual solitary waves and periodic wave trains over changing bottom topography with Chezy-law bottom friction. More significantly, it also makes it possible to investigate how these influences affect undular bores, which are inherently unsteady in the system being studied. The paper shows, in particular, that variable topography and bottom friction acting together typically place global constraints on undular bore motion. As a result, the leading solitary wave in an undular bore may evolve in a way that differs markedly from an isolated solitary wave of the same initial amplitude. This nonlocal behavior arises from nonlinear interactions among waves inside the undular bore and may produce extra growth in the solitary-wave amplitude, an effect that the conventional adiabatic theory for solitary-wave propagation in slowly varying media cannot foresee.

The paper investigates the propagation of shallow-water solitary waves and nonlinear periodic waves over gradually varying slopes in the presence of bottom friction. The analysis is based on a variable-coefficient Korteweg–de Vries (KdV) equation, which provides a mathematical model capable of capturing the combined effects of weak nonlinearity, weak dispersion, slowly varying bathymetry, and dissipative forces. In particular, the study focuses on situations where the bottom profile changes slowly compared with the characteristic wavelength, allowing asymptotic and modulation-based methods to be applied.

To analyze the wave evolution, the authors use the Whitham averaging method. This approach describes slowly varying nonlinear wave trains in terms of modulation equations for averaged quantities such as wave amplitude, mean level, wavelength, and phase velocity. The paper also incorporates recent advances in the Whitham theory for perturbed integrable systems, enabling the authors to treat effects such as variable topography and Chezy-law bottom friction in a systematic way. These perturbations modify the standard modulation equations and lead to more accurate predictions of wave evolution in realistic shallow-water environments.

A central contribution of the work is the improvement of existing theories for the adiabatic evolution of isolated solitary waves and nonlinear periodic wave trains. Traditional adiabatic theories describe how a solitary wave changes as it travels over slowly varying depth, often predicting amplitude growth or decay based on conservation laws and local wave parameters. By including both variable topography and bottom friction within a unified modulation framework, the authors refine these predictions and provide a more complete description of how waves respond to gradual shoaling, deepening, and dissipative losses.

The study also extends the analysis to undular bores, which are expanding oscillatory transition zones connecting two different mean water levels. Unlike isolated solitary waves or steady periodic wave trains, undular bores are inherently unsteady and involve a continuous range of nonlinear wave states. Their propagation is therefore influenced by variable topography and bottom friction in more complicated ways. The modulation approach makes it possible to track the evolution of the entire bore structure, including the leading solitary-wave-like edge, the trailing small-amplitude edge, and the interior nonlinear wave train.

One of the key findings is that the leading wave of an undular bore does not necessarily evolve in the same way as an isolated solitary wave traveling over the same bottom profile and subject to the same friction law. This difference arises because the leading wave is dynamically connected to the rest of the bore through nonlinear wave interactions and modulation effects. As a result, the combined influence of changing depth, bottom friction, and the internal dynamics of the undular bore can produce additional amplitude growth that is not predicted by traditional adiabatic solitary-wave theory. This highlights the importance of treating undular bores as full modulated wave structures rather than approximating their leading waves as independent solitary waves.

Overall, the paper provides a more comprehensive theoretical framework for understanding shallow-water nonlinear wave propagation in realistic environments. By combining variable-coefficient KdV modeling, Whitham modulation theory, and perturbation methods for integrable systems, the authors clarify how topography, friction, and nonlinear interactions jointly shape the evolution of solitary waves, periodic wave trains, and undular bores.

The paper investigates the evolution of nonlinear shallow-water waves as they propagate over slowly varying bottom topography in the presence of Chezy-type bottom friction. The main wave phenomena considered are isolated solitary waves, nonlinear periodic wavetrains, and undular bores. To describe these waves, the study uses a variable-coefficient Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation, which accounts for the effects of changing water depth and weak dissipation. The analysis is based on Whitham modulation theory, extended to perturbed integrable systems, allowing the authors to track the slow variation of wave parameters such as amplitude, mean level, wavelength, and bore edge speeds.

A central theme of the paper is the comparison between the behavior of an isolated solitary wave and the leading solitary wave of an undular bore. In classical adiabatic theory, a solitary wave traveling over a gradual slope adjusts locally to the changing depth and friction, with its amplitude determined mainly by the conditions at its current position. However, the paper shows that this local picture is incomplete for undular bores. Because an undular bore is an extended modulated wavetrain, its leading solitary wave is not governed only by local depth and friction. Instead, its evolution is constrained by the entire bore structure and by the global modulation conditions connecting the leading and trailing edges.

The study demonstrates that variable topography and bottom friction introduce nonlocal effects into the evolution of undular bores. These effects can cause the leading solitary wave of a bore to evolve in a way that differs significantly from an isolated solitary wave moving under the same environmental conditions. In some cases, the leading wave of the bore can grow more strongly than an isolated soliton would. This behavior arises because the bore’s modulation structure redistributes wave action and imposes integral constraints on the leading edge. As a result, the leading solitary wave reflects not merely the local balance between shoaling and frictional decay, but also the cumulative influence of the entire undular bore.

The paper therefore highlights an important limitation of traditional adiabatic solitary-wave theory when applied to complex nonlinear wavetrains. While adiabatic theory can successfully describe isolated waves over gradual slopes, it may fail to predict the amplitude and evolution of the leading waves in undular bores. By using Whitham averaging for perturbed integrable systems, the authors reveal how topography, friction, and nonlinear wave modulation combine to produce global interaction effects. These results improve the theoretical understanding of shallow-water wave transformation over variable beds and may be relevant to natural and experimental settings where tidal bores, internal bores, or long surface waves propagate through channels with changing depth and bottom resistance.
outputs.L5:
This text introduces the Korteweg–de Vries equation, often abbreviated as the KdV equation. It is a famous mathematical model used to describe waves in shallow water, especially long waves that travel without changing shape. The equation is named after Diederik Korteweg and Gustav de Vries, who studied it in the nineteenth century.

The Korteweg–de Vries equation is important because it explains the behavior of solitons. A soliton is a special type of wave that can move over long distances while keeping its form and speed. Even when solitons interact with each other, they can emerge afterward almost unchanged. This surprising property has made the KdV equation a central topic in applied mathematics, physics, and fluid dynamics.

Today, the Korteweg–de Vries equation is studied not only for water waves but also in areas such as plasma physics, nonlinear optics, and mathematical modeling. This shows how one equation, first connected to a practical physical problem, can become a powerful tool for understanding many natural phenomena.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a research paper on shallow-water solitary waves and undular bores propagating over a gradual slope with bottom friction, using a variable-coefficient KdV equation and Whitham averaging theory.
counterfactuals.output: We investigate the transformation of shallow-water solitary waves and undular bores propagating over a gradual bottom slope in the presence of bottom friction. The dynamics are modeled using a variable-coefficient Korteweg–de Vries (KdV) equation derived under the assumptions of weak nonlinearity, weak dispersion, slowly varying depth, and small dissipative effects. For solitary waves, an adiabatic perturbation approach is used to obtain evolution laws for amplitude, speed, and width, revealing the competing influences of shoaling-induced amplification and frictional attenuation. For undular bores, Whitham averaging theory is extended to include variable coefficients and weak dissipation, yielding modulation equations governing the spatial evolution of the bore edges, wavenumber, mean level, and wave amplitude. The analysis shows that gradual shoaling can enhance bore amplitude and shorten wavelength, while bottom friction reduces oscillation strength, modifies edge speeds, and may suppress bore development under sufficiently strong damping. Asymptotic predictions are compared with numerical solutions of the variable-coefficient KdV equation, demonstrating good agreement over slowly varying topography and identifying regimes where dissipation or slope-induced inhomogeneity becomes dominant. The results provide a unified framework for describing the evolution of nonlinear long-wave structures in coastal and estuarine environments and offer insight into the balance between topographic amplification, dispersive spreading, and frictional decay.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a formal journal-style abstract describing how Whitham modulation theory for perturbed integrable systems can be applied to nonlinear periodic waves, solitary waves, and undular bores in shallow water with variable topography and Chezy bottom friction.
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract**  
Whitham modulation theory provides a systematic asymptotic framework for describing the slow evolution of nonlinear wave trains in weakly perturbed integrable systems. This paper outlines its application to shallow-water waves propagating over variable topography in the presence of Chezy-type bottom friction. Starting from a perturbed integrable model, such as the Korteweg–de Vries equation with slowly varying depth and dissipative forcing, the periodic travelling-wave solution is parameterized by its Riemann invariants, and averaged conservation laws are used to derive a closed system of modulation equations with source terms representing bathymetric variation and frictional energy loss. The resulting perturbed Whitham system describes the adiabatic evolution of cnoidal waves, with important limiting reductions corresponding to solitary waves and small-amplitude harmonic waves. In the soliton limit, the modulation equations yield evolution laws for solitary-wave amplitude, speed, and width under shoaling and frictional attenuation. In the opposite limit, they recover linear wave-action balance over slowly varying depth. The same framework is also applicable to undular bores, where a rapidly oscillatory dispersive shock is represented as a slowly modulated nonlinear periodic wave connecting two mean flow states. Variable topography modifies the bore structure through shoaling-induced changes in amplitude and wavelength, while Chezy friction introduces irreversible decay and alters the bore’s leading- and trailing-edge speeds. This modulation-based description offers a unified analytical approach for nonlinear periodic waves, solitary waves, and undular bores in realistic shallow-water environments, extending classical integrable theory to weakly nonconservative and inhomogeneous settings relevant to coastal and hydraulic flows.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a theoretical study of shallow-water wave propagation over slowly varying bathymetry with friction, emphasizing the difference between isolated soliton evolution and the leading wave of an undular bore.
counterfactuals.output:
A theoretical study of shallow-water wave propagation over slowly varying bathymetry with bottom friction typically starts from the long-wave shallow-water equations and reduces them, under weak nonlinearity and weak dispersion, to a variable-coefficient KdV-type model with dissipative terms. The aim is to describe how nonlinear long waves evolve when the local depth changes gradually compared with the wavelength, while friction slowly removes energy.

The key physical setting is that depth variation alters the local wave speed, nonlinear coefficient, and dispersion coefficient. Friction introduces amplitude decay and modifies the balance between nonlinearity and dispersion. Because the bathymetry varies slowly, one can often use an adiabatic or modulation approach: at each position the wave is treated as being locally close to a known KdV structure, but with parameters that evolve according to conservation or balance laws.

For an **isolated soliton**, the evolution is comparatively simple. A soliton maintains its identity as a single coherent pulse, with its amplitude, width, and speed adjusting gradually to the changing depth and friction. In the absence of friction, shoaling over decreasing depth tends to amplify the soliton and narrow it, while increasing depth tends to reduce its amplitude and broaden it. With friction, this shoaling amplification is opposed by dissipative decay. Thus the soliton evolution is governed by a competition between bathymetric amplification and frictional damping. The result is an adiabatic law for the soliton amplitude, often expressible as a first-order evolution equation in distance or time.

The behavior of the **leading wave of an undular bore** is more subtle. An undular bore is not a single soliton but a modulated wavetrain connecting two different mean water levels. Its leading wave may look soliton-like, but it is embedded in a broader dispersive shock structure. Therefore its amplitude is not determined solely by local soliton balance. Instead, it is controlled by the modulation dynamics of the entire undular bore, including the jump conditions across the bore, the slowly varying mean flow, and the generation of oscillations behind the front.

This distinction is central. An isolated soliton evolves as an individual nonlinear wave conserving, or dissipating, its own invariants. The leading wave of an undular bore evolves as part of a collective structure whose amplitude depends on the bore strength and the modulation solution. Consequently, formulas derived for a solitary wave over variable depth generally cannot be applied directly to the first wave of an undular bore.

In particular, bathymetric shoaling can cause different trends for the two cases. A solitary wave may amplify according to a Green’s-law-like or KdV-soliton adiabatic scaling, modified by friction. The leading wave of an undular bore may amplify at a different rate, because the bore continuously redistributes mass, momentum, and energy among many oscillations. Friction further complicates this by damping the oscillatory train and reducing the bore strength, which can decrease the leading-wave amplitude even when shoaling alone would increase it.

Thus the study emphasizes that although the front of an undular bore resembles a soliton locally, it should not be treated as an isolated soliton. The correct description requires Whitham modulation theory, or an equivalent dispersive-shock framework, adapted to variable bathymetry and weak dissipation. The main conclusion is that slowly varying depth and friction affect isolated solitons and undular-bore fronts through different mechanisms: the former through adiabatic deformation of a single coherent pulse, the latter through modulation of an extended nonlinear wavetrain.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.output: We derive improved adiabatic asymptotics for Korteweg–de Vries solitary and cnoidal waves propagating over a slowly varying slope in the presence of weak bottom friction. By incorporating dissipative and topographic perturbations consistently into the modulation balance laws, we obtain corrected evolution equations for wave amplitude, mean level, phase speed, and elliptic modulus, extending classical shoaling predictions beyond conservative or locally forced approximations. The analysis shows that friction and depth variation couple through integral constraints, producing history-dependent corrections to wave parameters. Applied to undular bore evolution, the resulting Whitham-type description demonstrates that bore structure cannot be determined solely by local depth and dissipation: nonlocal accumulation of slope and friction effects modifies edge trajectories, wavelength distribution, and amplitude decay. These results clarify the limits of standard adiabatic theory and provide a more accurate framework for modeling nonlinear dispersive waves in coastal and shallow-water environments.

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a research-paper abstract about variable-coefficient Korteweg-de Vries modeling of nonlinear shallow-water waves, including Whitham averaging, Chezy friction, gradual slopes, and unexpected amplitude growth of leading solitary waves in undular bores.
counterfactuals.output: We investigate nonlinear shallow-water wave evolution over slowly varying bathymetry using a variable-coefficient Korteweg–de Vries (vcKdV) framework that incorporates weak nonlinearity, weak dispersion, gradual bottom slopes, and Chezy-type bottom friction. Starting from the long-wave asymptotic regime, we derive a forced-dissipative vcKdV equation in which spatial changes in depth modulate the nonlinear and dispersive coefficients while friction introduces amplitude-dependent damping. To describe rapidly oscillatory undular bore structures, Whitham modulation averaging is applied to the associated periodic traveling-wave solutions, yielding evolution equations for the slowly varying wave parameters across variable topography and dissipative environments. Particular attention is given to the leading solitary-wave edge of the bore, where standard expectations based on frictional attenuation can fail. The modulation analysis indicates that shoaling-induced changes in nonlinearity and dispersion may overcompensate Chezy dissipation, producing unexpected growth of the leading solitary-wave amplitude on gradual slopes. This growth is shown to depend sensitively on the balance among depth variation, bore strength, friction coefficient, and local Froude number. The results clarify mechanisms by which undular bores in rivers, estuaries, and coastal channels can maintain or amplify their foremost waves despite energy loss, with implications for field interpretation, hazard assessment, and reduced-order modeling of nonlinear shallow-water wave trains over realistic bathymetry.
